Protect Red Hat OpenShift Stateful Applications with Dell Container Storage Module on Dell PowerStore

This white paper provides guidance on protecting Red Hat OpenShift stateful applications deployed on Dell PowerStore during failure conditions, providing workload resiliency and continuity using Dell Container Storage Module (CSM) for Resiliency.

Appendix B: OpenShift network configuration YAML file

  • Here is an example of an OpenShift Ingress/API network configuration YAML file on a node. Modify the file as needed for your environment and then copy and paste it into the YAML editing box while configuring the static network using the Assisted Installer:

    interfaces:

     - name: ens2f0

     description: Ethernet ens2f0

     type: ethernet

     state: up

     ipv4:

     enabled: false

     mtu: 9000

     - name: ens3f0

     description: Ethernet ens3f0

     type: ethernet

     state: up

     ipv4:

     enabled: false

     mtu: 9000

     - name: bond0

     description: Bond with ports ens2f0 and ens3f0

     type: bond

     state: up

     ipv4:

     enabled: false

     link-aggregation:

     mode: 802.3ad

     options:

     miimon: "100"

     port:

     - ens2f0

     - ens3f0

     mtu: 1500

     - name: bond0.100

     description: vlan100 using bond0

     type: vlan

     state: up

     ipv4:

     address:

     - ip: 10.x.x.x

     prefix-length: 24

     enabled: true

     vlan:

     base-iface: bond0

     id: 100

     mtu: 1500

    routes:

     config:

     - destination: 0.0.0.0/0

     next-hop-address: 10.x.x.x

     next-hop-interface: bond0.100

    dns-resolver:

    config:

     search:

     - dell.local

     server:

     - 10.x.x.x

     - 10.x.x.x

Appendix C: Host network configuration YAML file

  • Here is an example of a host network configuration YAML file for creating bond1 between selected ports and passing VLAN:

    Create and apply the configuration on the OpenShift cluster.

    vi ocp-node1-bond1-vlans.yaml

    apiVersion: nmstate.io/v1

    kind: NodeNetworkConfigurationPolicy

    metadata:

     name: ocp-node1-bond1-vlans

    spec:

     nodeSelector:

       kubernetes.io/hostname: "ocp-node-1.dell.local"

     desiredState:

       interfaces:

       - name: ens2f1

         description: Ethernet ens2f1

         type: ethernet

         state: up

         ipv4:

           enabled: false

         mtu: 9000

       - name: ens3f1

         description: Ethernet ens3f1

         type: ethernet

         state: up

         ipv4:

           enabled: false

         mtu: 9000

       - name: bond1

         description: Bond using ports ens2f1 and ens3f1

         type: bond

         state: up

         ipv4:

           enabled: false

         link-aggregation:

           mode: 802.3ad

           options:

             miimon: '100'

           port:

           - ens2f1

           - ens3f1

         mtu: 9000

       - name: bond1.1078

         description: PowerStore Storage VLAN1078 using bond1

         type: vlan

         state: up

         ipv4:

            address:

           - ip: 192.168.78.22

             prefix-length: 24

           enabled: true

         vlan:

           base-iface: bond1

           id: 1078

    $kubectl apply -f ocp-node1-bond1-vlans.yaml

Appendix D: PostgreSQL YAML file

  • Here is an example of a YAML configuration file for a PostgreSQL database setup:

    kind: Service

    metadata:

      name: postgresql

      labels:

        app: postgresql

    spec:

      ports:

        - port: 5432

          targetPort: 5432

      selector:

        app: postgresql

    ---

    apiVersion: apps/v1

    kind: StatefulSet

    metadata:

      name: postgresql

      labels:

        app: postgresql

    spec:

      replicas: 1

      selector:

        matchLabels:

          app: postgresql

      template:

        metadata:

          labels:

            app: postgresql

            podmon.dellemc.com/driver: csi-powerstore

        spec:

          containers:

            - name: postgresql

              image: quay.io/anil_suraram/my-postgres:latest

              env:

                - name: POSTGRES_DB

                  value: mydb1

                - name: POSTGRES_USER

                  value: postgres

                - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD

                  valueFrom:

                    secretKeyRef:

                      name: postgresql-secret

                      key: POSTGRES_PASSWORD

              ports:

                - containerPort: 5432

              volumeMounts:

                - name: postgresql-pvc

                  mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data

          volumes:

            - name: postgresql-pvc

              persistentVolumeClaim:

                claimName: postgresql-pvc

    ---

    apiVersion: v1

    kind: PersistentVolumeClaim

    metadata:

      name: postgresql-pvc

    spec:

      accessModes:

        - ReadWriteOnce

      resources:

        requests:

          storage: 500Gi

      storageClassName: powerstore-xfs

    ---

    apiVersion: v1

    kind: Secret

    metadata:

      name: postgresql-secret

    type: Opaque

    data:

      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: cGFzc3dvcmQ=  # 'password' base64 encoded

    ---

    apiVersion: v1

    kind: ConfigMap

    metadata:

      name: postgresql-config

    data:

      pg_hba.conf: |

        # PostgreSQL Client Authentication Configuration File

        host all all 0.0.0.0/0 md5

      postgresql.conf: |

        listen_addresses = '*'

        max_connections = 100

Conclusion

  • This white paper provides guidance for deploying Dell CSI with the CSM Resiliency module in a Red Hat OpenShift cluster, using Dell PowerStore as the persistent storage backend. The focus is on enabling seamless failover, automated workload recovery, and continuous volume access during node failures and network disruptions for containerized applications running on Dell PowerStore. Overall, this solution empowers Kubernetes environments to achieve high availability and fault tolerance capabilities, ensuring business continuity and operational resilience without interruption.

Home > Storage > PowerStore > White Papers > Protect Red Hat OpenShift Stateful Applications with Dell Container Storage Module on Dell PowerStore > Configure the iSCSI initiator

Configure the iSCSI initiator

  • Follow the instructions below to configure the iSCSI initiator, perform target discovery, and establish a connection to the iSCSI target:

    1. On the OpenShift nodes, enable and start the iscsid service on each OpenShift node. This service is responsible for managing the iSCSI initiator. You can enable the service by running the following command on all worker nodes:

    # systemctl enable --now iscsid

    # systemctl start iscsid

    1. Make a note of the iSCSI initiator iSCSI Qualified Name (IQN). In the following example, it is iqn.1994-05.com.redhat:c15fd64bb4aa.

    # cat /etc/iscsi/initiatorname.iscsi

    InitiatorName=iqn.1994-05.com.redhat:c15fd64bb4aa

    1. Configure the iSCSI interface. The following command creates an iface file in the /var/lib/iscsi/ifaces/ directory:

    # sudo iscsiadm --m iface -I iface0 --o new

    1. Map the iface interface to the host NIC. In the following example, iface0 is the host NIC interface that will connect to the iSCSI target.

    # sudo iscsiadm --m iface -I iface0 -o update -n iface.net_ifacename -v vlan1078

    iface0 updated.

    1. Discover the PowerStore iSCSI target using the iface interface. In this example, it is iSCSI-NodeA: 192.168.78.3:

    # sudo iscsiadm -m discovery -t st -p 192.168.78.3:3260 -I iface0

    192.168.78.3:3260,1 iqn.2015-10.com.dell:dellemc-powerstore-apm00243410950-a-4e66d1de

    192.168.78.4:3260,1 iqn.2015-10.com.dell:dellemc-powerstore-apm00243410950-b-6120c3e5

    1. Log in to each of the iSCSI target nodes using the iface interface by running the

    iscsiadm command:

    # sudo iscsiadm -m node -T iqn.2015-10.com.dell:dellemc-powerstore-apm00243410950-a-4e66d1de -l iface0 -l

    1. Check the login session on the node by running the iscsiadm command:

    # sudo iscsiadm -m session

    tcp: [1] 192.168.78.3:3260,1 iqn.2015-10.com.dell:dellemc-powerstore-apm00243410950-a-4e66d1de (non-flash)

    tcp: [2] 192.168.78.4:3260,1 iqn.2015-10.com.dell:dellemc-powerstore-apm00243410950-b-6120c3e5 (non-flash)

    1. Enable multipathing for redundancy by running the following command:

    Cat <<EOF >/etc/multipath.conf defaults { user_friendly_names yes

    }

    devices { device {

    vendor "DellEMC" product "PowerStore"

    path_selector "queue-length 0" path_grouping_policy "group_by_prio" path_checker "tur"

    detect_prio "yes" failback "immediate" rr_min_io_rq 1

    hardware_handler "1 alua" prio "alua" fast_io_fail_tmo 15

    max_sectors_kb 1024

    }

    } EOF

    Enabling multipathing on OpenShift nodes ensures that the cluster can tolerate path failures and maintain uninterrupted access to Dell PowerStore storage systems by intelligently managing multiple I/O paths. For more details, see E-Lab Host Connectivity Guide for Linux.

    1. Enable and restart the multipath service:

    # systemctl enable --now multipathd

    # systemctl start multipathd

CSM Resiliency on Red Hat OpenShift with PostgreSQL

  • CSM for Resiliency provides intelligent monitoring and automated actions to ensure high availability of stateful applications in Kubernetes. It can detect failures and trigger appropriate recovery actions for the following failure scenarios:

    • Node Failure: Detects and responds to node crashes or unresponsiveness to prevent premature volume detachment and reduce I/O interruptions.
    • Kubernetes Control Plane Network Failure: Maintains volume attachments during temporary network disconnects between nodes and the control plane, helping avoid unnecessary failovers.
    • Kubernetes Control Plane Failure: Ensures application stability by preventing storage operations that could disrupt workloads during control plane outages.
    • Array I/O Network Failure: Detects data path disruptions between nodes and the PowerStore array and intelligently delays storage operations to allow transient issues to recover.

    Note: We validated how CSM Resiliency effectively handles various failover scenarios, as outlined above. This paper describes how CSM Resiliency responds to a node failure in a Red Hat OpenShift cluster by automatically recovering a PostgreSQL StatefulSet application, minimizing downtime and reducing the need for manual intervention.

CSM Resiliency

  • The Dell CSM for Resiliency is designed to enhance the fault tolerance and availability of Kubernetes-based applications that depend on persistent storage. As containerized workloads become increasingly critical to enterprise environments, maintaining data accessibility and application uptime during infrastructure failures is essential.

    At the core of the Dell CSM for Resiliency is the Pod Monitor, an integrated component that is designed to safeguard stateful applications from various failure scenarios, including node crashes, storage path disruptions, and control plane disconnects.

    CSM Resiliency is deployed as a sidecar named podmon alongside the CSI driver in both controller and node pods. These are referred to as controller-podmon and node-podmon, respectively.

CSM Resiliency

  • controller-podmon

    The controller-podmon component plays a critical role in maintaining the resiliency of stateful workloads by monitoring and managing CSM Resiliency-labeled pods across the cluster. Its key responsibilities include:

    • Watches for CSM Resiliency-labeled pods. If a pod is Initialized but Not Ready and scheduled on a node with a NoSchedule or NoExecute taint, controller-podmon invokes the controllerCleanupPod operation to remove the affected pod, enabling Kubernetes to reschedule a healthy replacement.
    • Periodically polls storage arrays to verify connectivity with nodes hosting CSM Resiliency-labeled pods. If connectivity is lost between an array and a node, controllerCleanupPod is triggered to clean up impacted pods that have lost I/O access.
    • Determines taint nodes to be unhealthy to prevent further pod scheduling. This also signals node-podmon to perform cleanup operations, ensuring that replaced pods cannot continue writing to their volumes.
    • If a CSM Resiliency labeled pod enters a CrashLoopBackOff state, controller-podmon deletes that pod so it can be replaced.

CSM Resiliency

  • node-podmon

    The node-podmon component operates on each node within the Kubernetes cluster and plays a key role in ensuring application-level resiliency for CSM-labeled stateful workloads. Its key responsibilities include:

    • Continuously watches for CSM Resiliency-labeled pods running on the local node. It tracks pod health and life cycle states to detect abnormalities such as CrashLoopBackOff, NotReady, or Unknown.
    • Observes the pod’s ability to interact with its persistent volume. If a pod loses I/O connectivity to the storage backend (PowerStore), node-podmon flags the pod as unhealthy.
    • When a pod is determined to be in a failed or degraded state, node-podmon signals controller-podmon to initiate the controllerCleanupPod process. This ensures that failed pods are deleted and volumes are properly handled.
    • If the node becomes tainted due to a failure, node-podmon ensures that any CSM Resiliency-labeled pods on that node are gracefully handled or removed to prevent volume corruption.

CSM Resiliency

  • controllerCleanupPod

    controllerCleanupPod takes the following actions:

    • Removes the unresponsive or unhealthy pod so that Kubernetes can create a new one.
    • Ensures the PowerStore volume is safely detached from the failed node to avoid data corruption.
    • Marks the failed node as a taint so no new pods are scheduled to it until it is fixed.
    • Prepare for automatic recovery, enabling Kubernetes to reschedule the pod on a healthy node and reattach the volume.

Dell PowerStore CSI/CSM

  • An important component outside of PowerStore that enables a flexible consumption model for Kubernetes is the PowerStore CSI driver, developed as a part of the Dell Kubernetes strategy. After loading the CSI driver for PowerStore into Kubernetes, the PowerStore CSI driver can be used to provision persistent volumes from the underlying PowerStore storage system. 

    The CSI driver connects the PowerStore system and Kubernetes deployments. It is a storage broker that dynamically provisions volumes from PowerStore through its API to the Kubernetes cluster. Once the volume is available on PowerStore, it is immediately mapped to the requesting pod. If a pod is destroyed or rescheduled, the CSI plug-in ensures that the volumes are remapped upon rescheduling of that pod. 

    Dell CSMs for PowerStore extend the standard CSI capabilities with additional key values, where each module is responsible for a different benefit. These modules help achieve the following: 

    • Observability: Provides visibility into storage performance and capacity through integration with tools like Prometheus and Grafana, allowing administrators to monitor metrics such as bandwidth, IOPS, and response times.
    • Replication: Enables replication and disaster recovery capabilities, allowing for the replication of volume groups and facilitating application restart in case of planned or unplanned migrations. 
    • Resiliency: Enhances the resilience of Kubernetes applications by detecting node failures, control plane network failures, and storage array I/O failures, and taking necessary actions to maintain application availability.
    • Application Mobility: Provides Kubernetes administrators with the ability to clone their stateful application workloads and application data to other clusters, either on-premises or in the cloud.

    For more information about CSM modules that are supported in PowerStore, see Dell CSM.

Deploy PostgreSQL

  • A PostgreSQL StatefulSet is deployed using a PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) backed by Dell PowerStore. The PostgreSQL pod is labeled with podmon.dellemc.com/driver: csi-powerstore, enabling the CSM Resiliency module’s PodMonitor to track pod health and respond to failures. The storage volume is dynamically provisioned through the PowerStore CSI driver, with CSM Resiliency enabled to ensure automated recovery and high availability in the event of node or pod-level disruptions.

    1. Run the following command to install the PostgreSQL StatefulSet application.

    # kubectl create -f <postgresql.yaml>

    For more information about the complete YAML file that is used to deploy a PostgreSQL StatefulSet with a PVC dynamically provisioned using the powerstore-xfs StorageClass and CSM Resiliency labels. For details, see the PostgreSQL YAML file.

    1. Verify that the PostgreSQL StatefulSet is up and running.

    # kubectl get statefulset postgresql

    NAME         READY   AGE

    postgresql   1/1     4s

    1. Patch an existing StatefulSet to include the podmon.dellemc.com/driver: csi-powerstore in the pod template, ensuring that all newly created pods from StatefulSet have this annotation.

    # kubectl patch statefulset/postgresql --type='merge' -p '{"spec": {"template": {"metadata": {"annotations": {"podmon.dellemc.com/driver": "csi-powerstore"}}}}}

    1. Verify that the PostgreSQL pod is associated with the StatefulSet.

    # kubectl get pods -l app=postgresql -o wide

    NAME           READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE   IP            NODE                     NOMINATED NODE   READINESS GATES

    postgresql-0   1/1     Running   0          15s   10.130.0.12   ocp-node-01.dell.local   <none>           <none>

    1. Verify the CSM Resiliency labels on the PostgreSQL pod.

    # kubectl get pods  --show-labels

    NAME           READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE   LABELS

    postgresql-0   1/1     Running   0          30s   app=postgresql,apps.kubernetes.io/pod-index=0,controller-revision-hash=postgresql-574dd7fcc8,podmon.dellemc.com/driver=csi-powerstore,statefulset.kubernetes.io/pod-name=postgresql-0

    1. Check that the Persistent Volume (PV) is correctly bound to the PostgreSQL StatefulSet.

    # kubectl get pv

    NAME                CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   RECLAIM POLICY   STATUS   CLAIM                    STORAGECLASS     VOLUMEATTRIBUTESCLASS   REASON   AGE

    csivol-41ec4c52f9    500Gi      RWO            Delete           Bound    default/postgresql-pvc   powerstore-xfs   <unset>                          40s

    1. Verify that the PVC for PostgreSQL is bound to the correct PV.

    # kubectl get pvc

    NAME             STATUS   VOLUME              CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   STORAGECLASS     VOLUMEATTRIBUTESCLASS   AGE

    postgresql-pvc   Bound    csivol-41ec4c52f9    500Gi      RWO            powerstore-xfs   <unset>                 50s

    1. Verify the volume details in the PowerStore Manager.
      1. Log in to the PowerStore Manager interface.
      2. Go to Storage > Volumes.
      3. Verify that the volume is created in the PowerStore Manager and is correctly mapped to a PV that is bound to the PostgreSQL.

    Figure 8.   Volume details in PowerStore Manager

    1. Click Host Mappings on the volume to verify the host mapping details of the volume that is created and that it is mapped to the OpenShift node where PostgreSQL runs.

    Figure 9.   Host map details in PowerStore Manager

    1. After the PostgreSQL StatefulSet is deployed, load sample data into the database.
      1. Get the name of the PostgreSQL pod and access the pod.

    # kubectl get pods -l app=postgresql

    # kubectl exec -it postgresql-0 -- /bin/bash

    1. Create a database using psql command.

    # psql -U postgres -d mydb1 -h localhost -p 5432 -W

    1. Insert the data into a database that is created using pgbench.

    # pgbench -h localhost -U postgres -d mydb1 -p 5432 -i -s 200

    1. Query the data.

    # psql -U postgres -d mydb1 -c "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM pgbench_accounts;"

      count

    ----------

     20000000

    (1 row)

Deployment steps

  • To deploy the OpenShift cluster:

    1. Log in to the Red Hat Hybrid Cloud Console.
    2. Click Create Cluster and go to the Datacenter tab.
    3. Click Create cluster and provide the following information:
      1. Enter the Cluster name and Base Domain. These details represent preconfigured environment-specific DNS entries.
      2. Select the supported OpenShift version that you require.

    Figure 4.   Creating a cluster using Assisted Installer

    1. As Static network configuration, select Host network configuration. This allows you to configure bonds and any required static network configuration upfront.
    2. Click Next.
    3. Select the YAML view option to configure the network using nmstate config, allowing advanced network configurations for the cluster nodes.
      1. Click Start from scratch in the YAML editing box and provide nmstate config in the YAML view. For details, see Static Network Configuration YAML file.
      2. Enter the MAC address for the first interface and the interface name in the Mac-to-interface name mapping section.
      3. Click the Add another MAC to interface name mapping button to enter the secondary interface details.
      4. Check the Copy the YAML content box and click the Add another host configuration button to enter the details of additional hosts.
      5. Modify the IP address in the YAML file and change the MAC address and Interface name in the boxes below it.
    4. After the network has been added for all the hosts, click Next.
    5. Under Operators, ignore the operators and click Next.
    6. Under Host Discovery, click Add hosts. Select the Minimal image file, enter an SSH public key for cluster nodes, and then click Generate Discovery ISO, as shown in the following figure:

    Figure 5.   Generating the discovery ISO

    1. Download the ISO and mount it to the iDRAC virtual media of the hosts. Boot the hosts from the virtual media.

    The installation process starts automatically, and the hosts are discovered in the Red Hat Hybrid Cloud Console.

    1. When the Status for each of the node’s changes to Ready, assign the roles (control plane or worker) to each of the nodes and click Next, as shown in the following figure:

    Figure 6.   Host Discovery

    1. In the Storage section, ensure that the correct bootable disks are chosen for formatting to proceed further and click Next.
    2. In the Networking section, select Cluster-Managed Networking and enter the available subnet, API IP, and Ingress IP details. Both the addresses must be preidentified and mapped to specific DNS entries for api. and *. apps respectively.
    3. Click Next.
    4. Review the configuration and click Install cluster.
    5. When the cluster deployment is complete, click Download kubeconfig to download the kubeconfig file and save the kubeadmin password. Use the web console URL to access the OpenShift web console, as shown in the following figure:

    Figure 7.   Cluster Installation status monitor

Executive summary

  • As enterprises accelerate the adoption of containerized platforms, ensuring the availability and resilience of persistent storage for stateful workloads has become a critical operational priority. While stateless microservices can scale and recover with minimal disruption, stateful applications such as databases and analytics engines require continuous, reliable access to storage systems. Dell’s Container Storage Module (CSM) for Resiliency, when integrated with Dell PowerStore, provides an enterprise-grade storage orchestration solution that is specifically designed to meet these needs. Together, they empower Kubernetes environments to deliver high availability, fault tolerance, and seamless failover capabilities, ensuring business continuity and operational resilience. 

    Red Hat OpenShift Container Platform offers enterprises full control over their Kubernetes environments, whether on-premises or in the public cloud, allowing teams to build and run containerized applications anywhere. Deploying OpenShift clusters on-premises traditionally requires significant manual effort. The OpenShift Assisted Installer simplifies this process, reducing the complexity associated with cluster deployment. 

    The Dell PowerStore platform uses a container-based microservices architecture, advanced storage technologies, and integrated machine learning to unlock the power of data. It is a versatile platform with a performance-centric design that provides multidimensional scale, always-on data reduction, and support for next-generation media. PowerStore brings the simplicity of public cloud to on-premises infrastructure, simplifying operations with an integrated machine-learning engine and seamless automation. It also offers predictive analytics to monitor, analyze, and troubleshoot the environment. PowerStore provides organizations with a data-centric, intelligent, and adaptable infrastructure that supports both traditional and modern workloads. 

    Dell’s Container Storage Module (CSM) for Resiliency enhances Kubernetes by introducing advanced storage intelligence that protects against infrastructure-level disruptions. CSM for Resiliency ensures that stateful applications maintain continuous access to persistent storage, even in the case of node failures, network partitions, or cluster reconfigurations. In cloud-native environments, this capability is essential for maintaining business continuity and ensuring consistent application availability. 

    This document provides deployment guidance for Dell’s CSM for Resiliency, leveraging the Red Hat OpenShift Container Platform and PostgreSQL on Dell PowerStore. This solution describes how CSM for Resiliency enables seamless failovers, automated recovery, and continuous data access, even during infrastructure failures or disruptions in Kubernetes environments.

Install PowerStore CSI driver with CSM Resiliency sidecar

  • Deployment steps

    To deploy the PowerStore CSI driver with CSM Resiliency on a Red Hat OpenShift cluster:

    1. Run the following command to download the installation source files from GitHub.

    # git clone -b v2.13.0 https://github.com/dell/csi-powerstore.git

    1. Run the following command to create the csi-powerstore namespace:

    # kubectl create namespace csi-powerstore

    1. Edit the samples/secret/secret.yaml file and configure connection information for your PowerStore arrays by changing the following parameters:

    # vi samples/secret.yaml

        endpoint: "https://10.x.x.1/api/rest"

        globalID: "PS8a9e82dd3e03"

        username: "admin"

        password: "xxxxxx"

        skipCertificateValidation: true

        blockProtocol: "ISCSI"

    Note: For more information about these parameters, see PowerStore CSI Documentation.

    1. Create the secret by running the following command:

    # kubectl create secret generic powerstore-config -n csi- powerstore --from-file=config=secret.yaml

    1. Create a storage class using examples from the samples/storageclass folder and apply them to the Kubernetes cluster by running:

    # kubectl create -f /csi- powerstore/samples/storageclass/powerstore-xfs.yaml

    This StorageClass will be used for dynamic provisioning of the PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) when deploying the PostgreSQL StatefulSet using the YAML file.

    1. Download the default values.yaml file by running:

    # cd dell-csi-helm-installer && wget -O my-powerstore- settings.yaml https://github.com/dell/helm-charts/raw/csi-powerstore-2.13.0/charts/csi-powerstore/values.yaml

    1. After downloading the values file from GitHub, edit the my-powerstore-setting.yaml file parameters to enable the CSM Resiliency module and change the value to true.

    podmon:

      enabled: true

      controller:

        args:

          - "--csisock=unix:/var/run/csi/csi.sock"

          - "--labelvalue=csi-powerstore"

          - "--arrayConnectivityPollRate=60"

          - "--driverPath=csi-powerstore.dellemc.com"

          - "--mode=controller"

          - "--skipArrayConnectionValidation=false"

          - "--driver-config-params=/powerstore-config-params/driver-config-params.yaml"

          - "--driverPodLabelValue=dell-storage"

          - "--ignoreVolumelessPods=false"

      node:

        args:

          - "--csisock=unix:/var/lib/kubelet/plugins/csi-powerstore.dellemc.com/csi_sock"

          - "--labelvalue=csi-powerstore"

          - "--arrayConnectivityPollRate=60"

          - "--driverPath=csi-powerstore.dellemc.com"

          - "--mode=node"

          - "--leaderelection=false"

          - "--driver-config-params=/powerstore-config-params/driver-config-params.yaml"

          - "--driverPodLabelValue=dell-storage"

          - "--ignoreVolumelessPods=false"

    Note: For more information about the instructions, see PowerStore CSM Resiliency documentation.

    1. Install the driver using the csi-install.sh bash script by running.

    # ./csi-install.sh --namespace csi-powerstore --values ./my- powerstore-settings.yaml

iSCSI connectivity

  • Prerequisites

    Ensure that the following conditions are met before configuring iSCSI on OpenShift nodes:

    • The storage network is properly configured on PowerStore.
    • VLAN IDs and subnets are correctly assigned.
    • On the iSCSI network interfaces, jumbo frames (MTU 9000) are enabled on both PowerStore and OpenShift nodes.
    • The iscsid service is enabled and persistent across reboots.
    • The network to access the iSCSI target is configured on the OpenShift nodes.

    For more information, see Create Block-optimized Storage networks in PowerStore Manager.

Logical architecture

  • The following diagram shows the logical architecture of this solution:

    Figure 2.   Logical architecture of CSM for Resiliency on Red Hat OpenShift with PowerStore

    An OpenShift cluster is deployed on three bare-metal nodes with the Red Hat OpenShift Assisted Installer. After deployment, necessary network configurations are applied to the OpenShift nodes. On OpenShift, nodes are configured with the iSCSI protocol to access PowerStore storage. PowerStore also supports the NVMe/TCP and FC protocols to access storage. For more information about the configuration of compute nodes used for the OpenShift cluster, see Appendix A Hardware and Software Configuration.

    The OpenShift cluster consists of:

    • OpenShift control plane: Manages the OpenShift Cluster, handles scheduling and API requests, and maintains the cluster state.
    • OpenShift worker: The computational power of the cluster, where applications operate and handle networking and container execution.
    • Infrastructure Host: The infrastructure host provides essential services that are required for the operation, accessibility, and management of the OpenShift cluster. These services typically include DNS, Active Directory, NTP, and a bastion node. The bastion node provides secure SSH access to the environment. It also hosts management tools such as the OpenShift CLI (oc) and kubectl, enabling administrators to interact with and manage the OpenShift cluster effectively.

    PowerStore supports both unified (block and file) and block-optimized (block-only) configurations with CSM Resiliency. This solution uses a PowerStore 5200T appliance that is configured as a block-optimized storage array, allowing the compute nodes to access storage using block protocols.

    The PowerStore platform features PowerStore Manager, an intuitive HTML5-based web interface designed for seamless cluster and appliance management. This user-friendly solution enables efficient monitoring and administration.

    The PowerStore CSI driver, along with the CSM Resiliency module, is installed on the OpenShift cluster to enable dynamic provisioning, high availability, and resilient management of storage volumes.

    The CSM for Resiliency includes a pod monitor (podmon) that detects failures such as node outages, control plane disruptions, and I/O network issues. It acts swiftly to clean up pod artifacts and revoke persistent volume (PV) access from failed nodes, preventing data corruption and ensuring that pods can be rescheduled on healthy nodes. The Resiliency module is deployed as a sidecar to the CSI driver in both the controller and node pods.

Network architecture

  • The following diagram shows the network architecture of this solution:

    Figure 3.   Network design of OpenShift nodes with Dell PowerStore

    At the physical layer, two supported Top of Rack (ToR) switches are used for redundancy and load-balancing purposes. A peer link is configured on both the ToR switches.

    PowerStore supports Ethernet connectivity through ports on the embedded module and on optional I/O modules. PowerStore supports FC connectivity through ports on optional I/O modules. The deployment in this paper covers only the iSCSI protocol.

    The network for storage services such as iSCSI, NVMe/TCP, and NAS is configured on PowerStore. PowerStore appliances require that Management, Storage/Replication, and NAS services each have unique network configurations. Dell Technologies highly recommends deploying PowerStore networks with multiple and unique VLANs to separate the traffic. For information about the storage service networking and configuration using PowerStore Manager, see Networking Guide for Storage Services.

    On the OpenShift nodes, two bond interfaces are created, each with two physical interfaces. VLAN subinterfaces are then created on top of these bonds to logically separate different traffic types. Jumbo frames are enabled (MTU: 9000) and are configured on both PowerStore and OpenShift nodes.

    For more information, see Appendix C Host Network Configuration.

    The following table shows the different networks that are configured for this solution:

Node failure

  • Node failure

    Node failures are among the most common and disruptive events in a Kubernetes cluster. These failures can be triggered by hardware issues, kernel panics, power outages, misconfigurations, or scheduled maintenance. Such disruptions can lead to I/O interruptions, temporary unavailability of persistent volumes, or degraded application performance, particularly impacting stateful applications running on Dell PowerStore storage.

    Dell CSM for Resiliency provides automated mechanisms to detect and respond to these failures, ensuring that PostgreSQL stateful applications can recover quickly and with minimal disruption. The CSM Resiliency framework continuously monitors all cluster nodes that host CSM-labeled pods.

    The below steps describe how CSM Resiliency responds to node failures.

    Note: The recovery actions are the same when CSM Resiliency responds to other failures, including Kubernetes Control Plane Network failure, Kubernetes Control Plane failure, and Array I/O Network failure.

    1. The CSM Resiliency module continuously monitors the status of all cluster nodes hosting CSM-labeled pods for the PostgreSQL application. It leverages Kubernetes node heartbeats and integrates with the Container Storage Interface (CSI) to detect unresponsive nodes.

    # kubectl get nodes

    NAME                     STATUS   ROLES                         AGE     VERSION

    ocp-node-01.dell.local   Ready    control-plane,master,worker   5d23h   v1.31.6

    ocp-node-02.dell.local   Ready    control-plane,master,worker   6d      v1.31.6

    ocp-node-03.dell.local   Ready    control-plane,master,worker   6d      v1.31.6

    1. Simulate a node failure in the Kubernetes cluster by shutting down a node.

    ssh core@ocp-node-01.dell.local

    sudo shutdown -h now

    1. When the Kubernetes control plane does not receive a heartbeat from a node for the duration that is specified by the node-monitor-grace-period (default: 15 minutes in some environments, though typically 40 seconds in most standard Kubernetes setups), the node is considered unreachable and is marked as NotReady and the taint node.kubernetes.io/unreachable:NoExecute is added to the node.

    # kubectl get nodes

    NAME                     STATUS     ROLES                         AGE   VERSION

    ocp-node-01.dell.local   NotReady   control-plane,master,worker   6d    v1.31.6

    ocp-node-02.dell.local   Ready      control-plane,master,worker   6d    v1.31.6

    ocp-node-03.dell.local   Ready      control-plane,master,worker   6d    v1.31.6

    # kubectl describe node ocp-node-01.dell.local | grep "Taints"

    Taints:             node.kubernetes.io/unreachable:NoExecute

    1. By default, Kubernetes StatefulSets waits for the existing PostgreSQL pod to be deleted before creating a new one. If the node hosting the PostgreSQL pod goes down, the pod cannot be deleted. As a result, Kubernetes waits indefinitely or until the failed node becomes available again. This behavior leads to PostgreSQL application downtime until an administrator manually intervenes to recover the service.
    2. With the CSM Resiliency module, where PostgreSQL pod is continuously monitored, PodMon detects node failures and automatically initiates the necessary recovery actions, ensuring minimal service disruption:
      1. CSM identifies the Persistent Volume Claims (PVCs) associated with the affected PostgreSQL pod and triggers a volume failover to a healthy node. This ensures that the volume becomes accessible on the new node.
      1. Kubernetes automatically reschedules the affected PostgreSQL pod onto a healthy node to restore functionality.
      2. Once rescheduled, the PostgreSQL pod restarts with access to the recovered volume, allowing the stateful PostgreSQL application to resume operation seamlessly.

    Figure 10.    PostgreSQL StatefulSet Recovery Workflow with CSM Resiliency 

    1. Check that the PostgreSQL pod is rescheduled to a healthy node and is in a running state.

    # kubectl get pods -o wide

    NAME           READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE   IP            NODE                     NOMINATED NODE   READINESS GATES

    postgresql-0   1/1     Running   0          27m   10.129.0.75   ocp-node-02.dell.local   <none>           <none>

    1. Verify the volume details in PowerStore Manager where it remaps the volume to the healthy node.
      1. Log in to the PowerStore Manager interface.
      1. Go to Storage > Volumes.
    1. Go to the volume mapped to Persistent Volume (PV) for the PostgreSQL and click Host Mappings.
    2. Verify that the volume is remapped to the healthy node.

    Figure 11.    Host remap details

    1. Access the PostgreSQL pod.

    # kubectl exec -it postgresql-0 -- /bin/bash

    1. Connect to the PostgreSQL database and verify that the same data is available after a node failure.

    # psql -U postgres -d mydb1 -c "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM pgbench_accounts;"

      count

    ----------

     20000000

    (1 row)

PowerStore

  • The PowerStore platform is a bare-metal unified storage array that can service block and file resources along with numerous data services and efficiencies. PowerStore is perfect for traditional and modern workloads, including relational databases, electronic medical record applications, and content repositories among many others.  

    PowerStore has two purpose-built platforms:

    • The 2U, two-node single-socket Intel® Xeon® platform: This platform is used for the PowerStore 500 model.
    • The 2U, two-node, dual- socket Intel® Xeon® platform: This platform is used for the PowerStore 1000, 1200, 3000, 3200, 5000, 5200, 7000, 9000, and 9200 models.

    They run the exact same version of software and can be clustered and managed together coherently. For more information about PowerStore platforms, see Dell PowerStore: Introduction to the Platform. 

    Figure 1.   PowerStore appliance

    Organizations that use new applications and solutions require dependable storage and often face the challenge of doing more with less. PowerStore addresses this challenge by packaging a powerful storage system into a cost-efficient and space-efficient profile. PowerStore features and benefits include: 

    • Active/active architecture 
    • Multiple protocol support including iSCSI, Fiber Channel, NVMe/FC, NVMe/TCP, SMB, FTP, SFTP, and NFS
    • Unified offering serving block and file storage 
    • Simplified, modern user interface 
    • Inline data reduction 
    • Local and remote native data protection 

    PowerStore achieves new levels of operational simplicity and agility. It uses container- based microservices architecture, advanced storage technologies, and integrated machine learning to unlock the power of your data. It offers predictive analytics to easily monitor, analyze, and troubleshoot the environment. PowerStore is highly adaptable, providing the flexibility to host specialized workloads and fits seamlessly into existing infrastructures to meet industry requirements. No matter where your business strategy takes you, PowerStore’s full-featured, adaptable design can help you build your unique breakthrough.

Prerequisites

  • Ensure that the following requirements are met. For more information, see OpenShift Assisted Installer prerequisites.

    • DNS: Records for ingress and API Virtual IP addresses (VIPs) are required for accessing the cluster. However, such VIPs are managed by the cluster itself, so no external load balancer is required.
    • SSH public key: Generate this key on the bastion node from where the OpenShift cluster nodes will be accessed. This key is used to authenticate SSH access to the OpenShift cluster nodes, for troubleshooting during deployment or for longer-term post-deployment maintenance. For more information about SSH key generation, see Generating a key pair for cluster node SSH access.
    • NTP server: For time synchronization among hosts.
    • Connectivity: As part of network requirements and because this deployment is the “connected” type, all the OpenShift cluster nodes must have connectivity to the Internet to retrieve container images, updates, and communicate with Red Hat services.

    Note: To install OpenShift in a disconnected environment, follow the instructions in Installing a cluster in a disconnected environment.

  • OpenShift Assisted Installer provides a SaaS-based managed service to deploy OpenShift clusters in various configurations, including bare metal servers and on-premises nodes, from the Red Hat Hybrid Cloud Console. For more information, see OpenShift Assisted Installer.

Verify the PowerStore CSI driver with CSM Resiliency sidecar

  • To verify the Dell CSI driver for PowerStore along with the CSM Resiliency sidecar deployment.

    1. Get the csi-powerstore namespace by running.

    # kubectl get namespace csi-powerstore

    NAME             STATUS   AGE

    csi-powerstore   Active   32h

    1. Verify Pods in the csi-powerstore namespace.

    # kubectl get pods -n csi-powerstore

    NAME                                     READY   STATUS    RESTARTS      AGE

    powerstore-controller-57db95f88c-lqp9t   8/8     Running   1 (9h ago)    9h

    powerstore-controller-57db95f88c-n8mrp   8/8     Running   1 (31h ago)   31h

    powerstore-node-clx4m                    3/3     Running   6             31h

    powerstore-node-t8r5k                    3/3     Running   0             31h

    powerstore-node-zr7dl                    3/3     Running   0             31h

    1. Verify that the CSI controller and node pods are running with the CSM Resiliency sidecar podmon.

    # kubectl get pod powerstore-controller-57db95f88c-lqp9t -n csi-powerstore -o jsonpath='{range .status.containerStatuses[*]}{.name}={": "}{.state}{"\n"}{end}'

    attacher=: {"running":{"startedAt":"2025-04-22T04:41:04Z"}}

    csi-metadata-retriever=: {"running":{"startedAt":"2025-04-22T04:41:20Z"}}

    dell-csi-replicator=: {"running":{"startedAt":"2025-04-22T04:41:21Z"}}

    driver=: {"running":{"startedAt":"2025-04-22T04:41:20Z"}}

    podmon=: {"running":{"startedAt":"2025-04-22T04:41:02Z"}}

    provisioner=: {"running":{"startedAt":"2025-04-22T04:41:10Z"}}

    resizer=: {"running":{"startedAt":"2025-04-22T04:41:07Z"}}

    snapshotter=: {"running":{"startedAt":"2025-04-22T04:41:12Z"}}
